title: My Calendar II
description: Brute force to optimized: per-time-unit counting versus tracking double-booked regions explicitly as intervals.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Implement a calendar that can add events, but prevents a TRIPLE booking (three events overlapping at any point in time). Implement book(start, end): return true and add the event if it does not cause a triple booking, otherwise return false and do not add it.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Prevent triple booking (double booking is OK)\"","Explicitly track all currently double-booked regions; reject a new event only if it overlaps one of THOSE"],["Interval overlap detection","Two events overlap if one starts before the other ends, in both directions"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Double bookings (two overlapping events) are explicitly allowed; only a THIRD overlapping event at the same point in time is forbidden. This means tracking not just individual bookings, but also every region that is ALREADY double-booked, lets a new event be checked directly against those regions: if it overlaps any of them, adding it would create a triple booking.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Meeting Room That Allows Sharing But Not Overcrowding
blocks.text: Picture a meeting room policy that allows two groups to share the room at once (double booking), but never a third group at the same time. Keeping a separate list of "currently double-booked time slots" lets you instantly check whether a new booking would push any of those slots into an overcrowded triple booking.

blocks.caption: Track both all bookings and all currently double-booked regions; reject only if the new booking overlaps a double region

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: book(10,20), book(50,60), book(10,40), book(5,15), book(5,10), book(25,55)
Results: true, true, true, false, true, true. book(5,15) is rejected since [10,15] would become a THIRD overlap with existing [10,20] and [10,40].
5. How Should We Think?

Before tracking every individual booked second, notice that maintaining a SEPARATE list of currently double-booked regions lets a new booking be checked in one pass: reject it if it overlaps ANY double region (would create a triple), otherwise accept it and record any NEW double-booked regions it creates with existing single bookings.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A triple booking occurs exactly when a new event overlaps a region that is ALREADY double-booked.

Observation 2: Maintaining a list of all currently double-booked regions (as intervals) lets a new event be checked against just this list first; if it overlaps any of them, reject it immediately.

Observation 3: If accepted, the new event might create NEW double-booked regions by overlapping with any EXISTING single booking; these overlaps should be computed and added to the double-booked list.

Observation 4: Finally, the new event itself is added to the list of all bookings, to be considered for future overlap checks.

This leads to maintaining two lists: all bookings, and all double-booked regions. A new event is rejected if it overlaps any double region; otherwise, its overlaps with existing bookings are recorded as new double regions, and it is added to the bookings list.
6. Brute Force Solution
Track every individual booked time unit in a map, counting how many events cover each unit, rejecting a new booking if it would push any unit's count to 3.
Why the code is written this way

items: Tracking individual time units directly and correctly detects triple bookings.
This costs time proportional to event DURATION (which can be huge), not just the number of events, making it impractical for long events.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(duration) per booking.
Space: O(total time range) for the counts map.
Limitation: tracking double-booked REGIONS as intervals (rather than individual time units) makes each check cost O(number of existing bookings), independent of event duration.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Maintain two interval lists: all bookings, and all double-booked regions. For a new booking, first check it against the double-booked list; if it overlaps any of them, reject it (a third overlap would occur). Otherwise, compute its overlap with every EXISTING booking, adding each such overlap as a new double-booked region, then add the new booking itself to the bookings list.
Check against the double-booked list first (reject on overlap); otherwise compute and record new double-booked regions from overlaps with existing bookings; add the new event to the bookings list.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for book(10,20), book(50,60), book(10,40)

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since only regions ALREADY double-booked can turn into a triple booking, checking a new event against just that list correctly identifies whether it should be rejected. If accepted, computing its overlap with every existing single booking correctly identifies every NEW region that becomes double-booked as a result, keeping the overlaps list accurate for future checks.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per booking, n being the number of existing bookings.
Space: O(n squared) worst case for the overlaps list.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

My Calendar II demonstrates explicitly tracking a DERIVED structure (double-booked regions), not just the raw bookings, to make the actual constraint check (avoiding triple booking) direct and efficient.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to check against the double-booked regions FIRST, before computing new overlaps, which could incorrectly accept a triple-booking event.
Using non-strict inequalities inconsistently, mishandling events that touch but do not truly overlap.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Events that touch exactly (one ends when another starts)","Not considered overlapping."],["The very first booking","Always succeeds, since no overlaps or double regions exist yet."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly explaining "we track double-booked regions SEPARATELY, so a triple-booking check is just an overlap check against that list" clarifies the key design insight.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "allow double booking but not triple", think: explicitly track double-booked regions, reject only if the new event overlaps one.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you extend this to My Calendar III, allowing any number of overlaps but tracking the MAXIMUM concurrent bookings?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: My Calendar I (the simpler no-overlap-at-all version) and My Calendar III (tracking max overlap count), forming a natural progression of this technique.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Per-time-unit counting costs O(duration) per call; the two-interval-list approach costs O(n) per call, both against the number of existing bookings, the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: explicitly track a derived structure (double-booked regions) to make the actual constraint check direct.
Core Idea: reject a new booking if it overlaps any double-booked region; otherwise, record new double regions from overlaps with existing single bookings.
Time: O(duration) per call for the brute force, O(n) per call for the optimized approach.
Space: O(total time range) versus O(n squared) worst case.
Most Important Observation: only regions ALREADY double-booked can become triple-booked, so tracking them explicitly directly answers the actual question.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known interval design problem, testing careful state tracking.
One line memory trick: track double-booked regions separately; reject only if the new event overlaps one.
